- $P(x):$ $x$ is divisible by $6.$

- $Q(x):$ $x$ is even.

Then, our initial sentence can be written as $P(x)⇒Q(x),$ which is logically equivalent to 

$$
¬P(x)∨Q(x).
$$

The negation of $P(x)$ can be written as

- $¬P(x):$ $x$ is not divisible by $6.$

Therefore, the given sentence is logically equivalent to the following:

$\,$ $x$ is not divisible by $6,$ or $x$ is even." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b00e9ccc-cb21-5b11-b471-3e4372943962"] :db/ensure $$

$$

Now, we note the following:

- The truth set of $P(x)$ is 

$$
{T}_{P}={2,4,6,8,10}.
$$

As a result, the complement is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\overset{―}{T}}_{P} & =\overset{―}{{2,4,6,8,10}} \\  & ={1,3,5,7,9}.\end{aligned}
$$

- The truth set of $Q(x)$ is 

$$
{T}_{Q}={1,2,3,4,6}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}_{P⇒Q} & ={\overset{―}{T}}_{P}\cup {T}_{Q} \\  & ={1,3,5,7,9}\cup {1,2,3,4,6} \\  & ={1,2,3,4,5,6,7,9}.\end{aligned}

- $x\in Z$ if and only if $-x\in Z.$

- $x\in Z$ is equivalent to $-x\in Z.$

- If $x\in Z$ then $-x\in Z$, and if $-x\in Z$ then $x\in Z.$

Note that we're assuming our predicates have the same universal set.

The **implication** of the predicates $P$ and $Q$ is a new predicate that we denote as follows: $$P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n) \Rightarrow Q(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$$

This implication is false whenever $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ is true *and* $Q(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ is false for a specific set of respective variable assignments $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n.$

Now, recall the following logical equivalence:

$$P\Rightarrow Q \equiv \lnot P \lor Q$$

Therefore, the truth set of $P \Rightarrow Q$ is given by

$$\begin{aligned}{T}_{P\Rightarrow Q} & ={T}_{¬P∨Q} \\ & ={T}_{¬P}\cup {T}_{Q} \\ & ={\overset{―}{T}}_{P}\cup {T}_{Q}.\end{aligned}$$

For example, suppose we have the following universal set:

$$U = \big\{ 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9 \big\}$$

Let's define the following predicates over $U{:}$

- $P(x):$ $x$ is prime
- $Q(x):$ $9$ is divisible by $x$

To find the truth set of $P(x) \Rightarrow Q(x),$ we note the following:

- The truth set of $P(x)$ is $T_P = \left\{ 2,3,5,7 \right\}.$ As a result, the complement is $$\begin{aligned}{\overset{―}{T}}_{P}=\overset{―}{{2,3,5,7}}={1,4,6,8,9}.\end{aligned}$$
- The truth set of $Q(x)$ is $$T_Q = \big\{ 1,3,9 \big\}.$$

Therefore, we have

$$\begin{aligned}{T}_{P\Rightarrow Q} & ={\overset{―}{T}}_{P}\cup {T}_{Q} \\ & ={1,4,6,8,9}\cup {1,3,9} \\ & ={1,3,4,6,8,9}.\end{aligned}$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "06a295ff-82fc-5afe-8aa1-b24421f2c474" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7992 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "49a55e7b-da8f-5b9b-aca0-ea5672a75f90" :step/math-academy-id 144906 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199058}} {:db/id 17592186199058 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198265 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198114 :question/id #uuid "662bda92-63ee-5d5c-a45f-7219b160e08d" :question/math-academy-id "e-12740"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "264cfe66-691e-550e-97ad-b71924332f21" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049176} {:db/id 17592186049552} {:db/id 17592186049811}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186198718} {:db/id 17592186198719} {:db/id 17592186381643} {:db/id 17592186381650} {:db/id 17592186381657} {:db/id 17592186381664}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Truth Set of an Implication"} :step/id #uuid "5bf2cacb-1ce2-5c76-9cc6-0e6f2a29dc49" :step/math-academy-id 144907 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199059}} {:db/id 17592186199059 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199533 :tutorial/content "Let $T_P$ and $T_Q$ be the truth sets of the predicates $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ and $Q(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n),$ respectively. Again, we're assuming our predicates have the same universal set.

The **equivalence** of the predicates $P$ and $Q$ is a new predicate that we denote as follows: $$P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n) \Leftrightarrow Q(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$$

This predicate is true when $P$ and $Q$ have the same truth values for a specific set of variable assignments $x_1,x_2,\ldots, x_n.$

$$P \Leftrightarrow Q \equiv \big(P \land Q\big) \lor \big(\neg P \land \neg Q\big)$$

Let's look at some examples. Assume $x\in\mathbb R$ throughout.

- The following statement is an equivalence (i.e., it is true). $$x + 2 = 5 \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad x=3$$ This statement is true because $$\left(x+2=5\quad\Rightarrow\quad x=3\right)\qquad\textrm{and}\qquad \left(x=3\quad\Rightarrow\quad x+2 = 5\right).$$
- The following statement is **not** an equivalence (i.e., it is false). $$x^2 = 4 \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad x=2$$ This statement is false because $$\left(x=2 \quad \Rightarrow\quad x^2 = 4\right) \qquad \textrm{and} \qquad \left(x^2=4\quad \not\Rightarrow\quad x=2\right).$$ However, the following statement is true: $$x^2 = 4 \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad x=\pm 2$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5e9f21f0-8dbb-5442-968e-b1fb4425fef7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7995 :tutorial/title "Equivalence of Predicates"} :step/id #uuid "62147a48-4a50-55e4-a548-b950bc9af5a9" :step/math-academy-id 144910 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199060}} {:db/id 17592186199060 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199609 :tutorial/content "For predicates $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ and $Q(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n),$ the equivalence $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)\Leftrightarrow Q(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ is true when $P$ and $Q$ have the same truth value.

$$P \Leftrightarrow Q \equiv \big(P \land Q\big) \lor \big(\neg P \land \neg Q\big)$$

It follows that the truth set of $P \Leftrightarrow Q$ can be found using

$$\begin{aligned}{T}_{P⇔Q}=({T}_{P}\cap {T}_{Q})\cup ({\overset{―}{T}}_{P}\cap {\overset{―}{T}}_{Q}).\end{aligned}$$

Let's find the truth set of $P(x) \Leftrightarrow Q(x)$ given the following predicates defined over the universal set $\mathbb{R}{:}$

- $P(x):$ $1-5x < 11$
- $Q(x):$ $x \geq -1$

Note the following:

- To find the the truth set of $P(x),$ we solve the corresponding inequality: $$\begin{aligned}1-5x & <11 \\ -5x & <10 \\ x & >-2\end{aligned}$$ So, the truth set of $P(x)$ is $T_P = (-2, \infty)$ and its complement is $\overline{T}_P = (-\infty,-2].$
- The truth set of $Q(x)$ is $T_Q = [-1, \infty)$ and its complement is $\overline{T}_Q = (-\infty,-1).$

Therefore, we have

$$\begin{aligned}{T}_{P}\cap {T}_{Q} & =(-2,\infty )\cap [-1,\infty ) \\ & =[-1,\infty ) \\ {\overset{―}{T}}_{P}\cap {\overset{―}{T}}_{Q} & =(-\infty ,-2]\cap (-\infty ,-1) \\ & =(-\infty ,-2] \\ {T}_{P⇔Q} & =({T}_{P}\cap {T}_{Q})\cup ({\overset{―}{T}}_{P}\cap {\overset{―}{T}}_{Q}) \\ & =[-1,\infty )\cup (-\infty ,-2] \\ & =(-\infty ,-2]\cup [-1,\infty ).\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}P\Rightarrow Q & ≡¬P∨Q \\ P⇔Q & ≡(P\Rightarrow Q)∧(Q\Rightarrow P) \\ & ≡(¬P∨Q)∧(¬Q∨P) \\ & ≡(¬P∧¬Q)∨(P∧Q)\end{aligned}$$

For conditional statements, the following are equivalent:

- $P\Rightarrow Q$
- *If $P,$ then $Q$*
- *$P$ implies $Q$*

For biconditional statements, the following are equivalent:

- $P\Leftrightarrow Q$
- *$P$ is equivalent to $Q$*
- *$P$ if and only if $Q$*
- *If $P$ then $Q,$ and if $Q$ then $P$*" :tutorial/id #uuid "599dc11e-cbd2-596c-bb72-4f73b83034ab" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7993 :tutorial/title "Logical Laws Involving Implications and Equivalences With Predicates"} :step/id #uuid "b35ba584-56c8-537f-b6d7-15de6671592a" :step/math-academy-id 144915 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199063}} {:db/id 17592186199063 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198267 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198113 :question/id #uuid "316efd8a-8618-58b9-a41c-7507942f15b4" :question/math-academy-id "e-12739"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0d6db336-845a-506a-b020-cced1b38e23a" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186198716} {:db/id 17592186198717} {:db/id 17592186381671} {:db/id 17592186381678} {:db/id 17592186381685} {:db/id 17592186401755}] :knowledge-point/title "Using Laws Involving Implications and Equivalences"} :step/id #uuid "bc5d356c-d8d2-517d-839c-18b823820728" :step/math-academy-id 144916}] :activity/title "Conditional Statements With Predicates" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186198522} {:db/id 17592186199057 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199531 :tutorial/content "Let $T_P$ and $T_Q$ be the truth sets of the predicates $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ and $Q(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n),$ respectively. By the end of the course, students will appreciate how set theory provides a comprehensive toolkit for proving mathematical results.
After mastering these fundamentals, students will explore various proof-writing techniques, including direct proof, proof by cases, proof by contrapositive, proof by contradiction, disproof, and mathematical induction.
